EMOTIONAL-DISTRESS CLAIMS ARISING FROM A TERMINATION AND THE WORKERS’ COMPENSATION EXCLUSIVE REMEDY (LAB. CODE §§ 3600, 3601, 3602, 3208.3; COLE V. FAIR OAKS FIRE PROTECTION DIST.; SHOEMAKER V. MYERS; LIVITSANOS V. SUPERIOR COURT; MIKLOSY V. REGENTS; CITY OF MOORPARK V. SUPERIOR COURT; LIGHT V. DEPARTMENT OF PARKS & RECREATION) — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Jordan Lee · Acme, Inc.

SCOPE OF THIS INFORMATION SHEET
This information sheet describes how California law treats a claim for emotional-distress damages that arises out of the way an employment ended — the workers’ compensation exclusive remedy, the categories of employer conduct California courts have placed inside and outside the “compensation bargain,” and the separate Labor Code rules that govern when a psychiatric injury is compensable through the workers’ compensation system at all. It is prepared in connection with the separation of Jordan Lee from Acme, Inc., where the position held is stated as Field Technician, notice of termination or layoff is stated to have been given on June 12, 2026, and the employment is stated to have ended on July 10, 2026. Those facts are as supplied by the person preparing this sheet; nothing here verifies them. This sheet describes published California statutes and published California appellate decisions. It is not a workers’ compensation claim form, not a civil complaint, not a court filing, and not a determination that any claim exists, that any claim is or is not barred, or that any injury occurred.

THE COMPENSATION BARGAIN AND THE EXCLUSIVE REMEDY PROVISIONS
California’s workers’ compensation system rests on a trade the California Supreme Court calls the “compensation bargain.” Labor Code section 3600, subdivision (a) imposes liability for workers’ compensation on an employer, without regard to negligence, for injuries arising out of and in the course of employment where the listed conditions of compensation concur, and it does so “in lieu of any other liability whatsoever” except as specifically provided in sections 3602, 3706 and 4558. Labor Code section 3602, subdivision (a) states the consequence: where section 3600’s conditions concur, the right to recover compensation is the sole and exclusive remedy of the employee against the employer. In Shoemaker v. Myers the Court described the theory behind those provisions — the employer takes on liability for industrial injury without regard to fault in exchange for a cap on the amount, and the employee gets relatively swift and certain benefits without having to prove fault but gives up the wider range of damages potentially available in tort. Section 3602, subdivision (c) marks the outer edge of the rule: in all cases where section 3600’s conditions of compensation do not concur, the employer’s liability is the same as if the workers’ compensation division had not been enacted. Whether the conditions of compensation concur as to any injury claimed by Jordan Lee is not addressed here.

COLE V. FAIR OAKS: CONDUCT THAT IS A “NORMAL PART OF THE EMPLOYMENT RELATIONSHIP”
Cole v. Fair Oaks Fire Protection Dist. is the decision that set the test. A fire captain alleged that his assistant chief harassed him over union activity, falsely accused him of dishonesty, put him through what the complaint called a “kangaroo” disciplinary proceeding, publicly demoted him and stripped him of his badge, assigned him menial duties, and applied to force him into involuntary retirement; the stress raised his blood pressure and he suffered a disabling stroke. The California Supreme Court held the claim belonged in the workers’ compensation system. Its reasoning was that where the misconduct attributed to the employer consists of actions that are a normal part of the employment relationship — the Court named demotions, promotions, criticism of work practices, and frictions in negotiations as to grievances — an employee whose emotional distress causes disability cannot escape the exclusive remedy provisions by relabeling the employer’s decisions as manifestly unfair, outrageous, harassment, or intended to cause emotional disturbance. The Court explained why: if calling ordinary workplace conduct unfair or outrageous were enough, an employee could plead around exclusivity in every case merely by alleging an ulterior purpose of causing injury, which would be contrary to the compensation bargain. Applying that test to the facts before it, the Court described disciplinary hearings, demotions, friction over grievances, decisions to seek disability retirement, and demands to attend meetings that interfere with personal arrangements as an inherent part of the employment setting. How this test applies to anything that occurred between Jordan Lee and Acme, Inc. is not evaluated here.

SHOEMAKER V. MYERS: THE DISCHARGE ITSELF IS ORDINARILY INSIDE THE BARGAIN
Cole involved discipline and demotion rather than a discharge. Shoemaker v. Myers extended the reasoning to the termination itself. A state investigator alleged he was fired in retaliation for reporting wrongdoing, and pleaded causes of action for wrongful termination and related torts along with allegations of resulting physical illness and disability. The California Supreme Court held that disabling injuries, whether physical or mental, arising from termination of employment are generally within the coverage of workers’ compensation and subject to the exclusive remedy provisions, unless the discharge comes within an express or implied statutory exception or results from risks reasonably deemed not to be within the compensation bargain. The Court reached that result by comparing the discharge to the list in Cole: it had held there that demotion, transfer, discipline, and even an attempt to force an employee into involuntary retirement were within the ambit of workers’ compensation, and it reasoned that a nonconsensual termination is indistinguishable from those actions and must likewise be considered a normal and inherent part of employment. Shoemaker also observed that the reach of the phrase “arising out of and in the course of the employment” is not cut off by the discharge itself, pointing to cases treating injuries suffered after a discharge — while retrieving tools or personal effects, or while discussing the reasons for the firing — as compensable. What this means for the separation of Jordan Lee on July 10, 2026 is not evaluated here.

LIVITSANOS V. SUPERIOR COURT: A PURELY EMOTIONAL INJURY IS TREATED THE SAME WAY
For a time some Court of Appeal decisions drew a line between “physical” and “emotional” harm, reasoning that a claim for purely emotional injury fell outside the workers’ compensation scheme and could be litigated as a tort. Livitsanos v. Superior Court rejected that line. A terminated executive alleged a campaign of harassment resulting in the wrongful termination of his employment and pleaded intentional and negligent infliction of emotional distress without alleging any physical disability. The California Supreme Court held that claims for intentional or negligent infliction of emotional distress are preempted by the exclusivity provisions of the workers’ compensation law notwithstanding the absence of any compensable physical disability. The Court called the physical-versus-emotional dichotomy logically insupportable and pointed out the perverse incentive it created, since the more severe the employer’s conduct and the more disabling the resulting distress, the more likely the employer would be shielded. It framed the governing rule instead in terms of two exceptions: so long as the basic conditions of compensation are otherwise satisfied and the employer’s conduct neither contravenes fundamental public policy nor exceeds the risks inherent in the employment relationship, an employee’s emotional distress injuries are subsumed under the exclusive remedy provisions. The Court also noted that the injury must still result in an industrial disability compensable under the workers’ compensation law. Whether any of this describes a claim of Jordan Lee is not addressed here.

THE TWO RECOGNIZED EXCEPTIONS: OUTSIDE THE COMPENSATION BARGAIN
The exclusive remedy provisions do not reach every injury that happens at work. Shoemaker v. Myers collected the ways California courts have described the boundary, identifying the exclusive remedy provisions as inapplicable to conduct where the employer or insurer stepped out of their proper roles, or to conduct of an employer having a questionable relationship to the employment, and defining the category as conduct not stemming from a risk reasonably encompassed within the compensation bargain. Light v. Department of Parks & Recreation restates the analysis as a two-step inquiry taken from Charles J. Vacanti, M.D., Inc. v. State Comp. Ins. Fund: first ask whether the alleged injury falls within the scope of the exclusive remedy provisions, and if it does, ask whether the acts or motives that establish the elements of the cause of action fall outside the risks encompassed within the compensation bargain — with the cause of action barred where the acts are a normal part of the employment relationship or the workers’ compensation claims process, or where the motive behind them does not violate a fundamental policy of this state, and allowed to go forward if not. Shoemaker itself applied that boundary to hold that an injury from a termination in retaliation for protected whistleblowing under the statute then before the Court lay well outside the compensation bargain. Which side of that line any conduct involving Jordan Lee falls on is not evaluated here.

MIKLOSY V. REGENTS: A SURVIVING WRONGFUL-DISCHARGE CLAIM DOES NOT CARRY THE DISTRESS CLAIM WITH IT
A common assumption is that if a discharge was unlawful, every tort claim arising from it escapes the exclusivity bar. Miklosy v. Regents of the University of California shows that the two questions are separate. Laboratory employees sued for whistleblower retaliation, wrongful and constructive wrongful termination in violation of public policy, and intentional infliction of emotional distress. The California Supreme Court held the distress claims barred, reasoning that the alleged wrongful conduct occurred at the worksite, in the normal course of the employer-employee relationship, and that workers’ compensation was therefore the exclusive remedy for any resulting injury. The Court addressed the two Livitsanos exceptions directly. The public-policy exception, it explained, is aimed at permitting a Tameny action to proceed despite the exclusive remedy rule — that is, it preserves the wrongful-discharge tort itself, not a separate distress claim. As to the exception for conduct exceeding the risks inherent in the employment relationship, the Court acknowledged it might seem at first blush to apply to whistleblower retaliation but said it had rejected that same argument in Shoemaker. Miklosy also reproduced the Shoemaker passage holding that the kinds of conduct at issue, such as discipline or criticism, are a normal part of the employment relationship, and that even if characterized as intentional, unfair or outrageous, such conduct is nevertheless covered by the exclusivity provisions. Nothing in this clause states which causes of action, if any, Jordan Lee has.

DISTRESS CLAIMS FOUNDED ON FEHA-PROHIBITED DISCRIMINATION OR RETALIATION
A separate line of California decisions treats emotional-distress claims founded on unlawful discrimination or retaliation differently from claims founded on ordinary personnel decisions. Light v. Department of Parks & Recreation collects that line and follows it. The Court of Appeal concluded that the workers’ compensation system was not the exclusive remedy for the plaintiff’s alleged injuries because they were based on conduct prohibited by the Fair Employment and Housing Act. It quoted Accardi v. Superior Court for the proposition that emotional distress caused by misconduct in employment relations involving promotions, demotions, criticism of work practices and negotiations as to grievances is a normal part of the employment environment and is barred, but that the Legislature did not intend that an employer be allowed to raise the exclusivity rule for the purpose of deflecting a claim of discriminatory practices. Light acknowledged that Division Three of the same appellate district had read Miklosy in Yau v. Santa Margarita Ford, Inc. to allow only a single exception, for Tameny claims, and said it believed Yau reads Miklosy too narrowly — reasoning that Miklosy expressly retained the exception for conduct exceeding the risks inherent in the employment relationship and had not considered the body of case law holding that conduct violating the Fair Employment and Housing Act is not part of the employment relationship or the compensation bargain. Light concluded that, absent further guidance from the California Supreme Court, it was unwilling to abandon the longstanding view that unlawful discrimination and retaliation in violation of that Act falls outside the compensation bargain. Whether any conduct toward Jordan Lee was discrimination or retaliation is not addressed here.

CITY OF MOORPARK: THE EXCLUSIVE REMEDY PROVISIONS REACH ONLY DIVISION 4 REMEDIES
City of Moorpark v. Superior Court supplies a textual reason why statutory discrimination remedies are not swept into the workers’ compensation bar. A city employee was terminated after knee surgery and sued for disability discrimination under the Fair Employment and Housing Act and for common law wrongful discharge; the city argued that because her disability was work related, Labor Code section 132a was her exclusive remedy. The California Supreme Court disagreed, holding that section 132a does not provide the exclusive remedy for that type of discrimination and that Fair Employment and Housing Act and common law remedies are available. Part of its reasoning was structural. Labor Code section 3600 speaks of liability for “the compensation provided by this division,” and section 3207 defines compensation as compensation under division 4 of the Labor Code; section 132a sits in division 1. The Court concluded that the plain language of the exclusive remedy provisions apparently limits those provisions to division 4 remedies, and that remedies the Legislature placed in other divisions of the Labor Code are simply not subject to the workers’ compensation exclusive remedy provisions. WHEN A PSYCHIATRIC INJURY IS COMPENSABLE INSIDE THE SYSTEM AT ALL
Saying that the workers’ compensation system is the exclusive remedy for a distress injury is not the same as saying the system will pay for it. Subdivision (a) makes a psychiatric injury compensable if it is a mental disorder that causes disability or need for medical treatment and it is diagnosed under the prescribed criteria. Subdivision (b)(1) requires the employee to demonstrate by a preponderance of the evidence that actual events of employment were predominant as to all causes combined of the psychiatric injury, and subdivision (b)(2) lowers that showing to “a substantial cause” — defined in subdivision (b)(3) as at least 35 to 40 percent of the causation from all sources combined — for employees whose injuries resulted from being a victim of a violent act or from direct exposure to a significant violent act. Subdivision (c) states the Legislature’s intent to establish a new and higher threshold of compensability for psychiatric injury. Subdivision (d) bars compensation for a psychiatric injury unless the employee has been employed by that employer for at least six months, which need not be continuous, and does not apply where the injury is caused by a sudden and extraordinary employment condition; the same subdivision adds that nothing in it authorizes a damages action that would not otherwise exist under the exclusive remedy doctrine. Whether any injury claimed by Jordan Lee meets any of these thresholds is not evaluated here.

THE GOOD-FAITH PERSONNEL ACTION DEFENSE
Labor Code section 3208.3, subdivision (h) contains the provision that most often decides a psychiatric-injury claim built on a discharge. SUING THE SUPERVISOR INDIVIDUALLY: LABOR CODE SECTION 3601
Employees who believe a particular manager caused the distress sometimes name that manager personally. Labor Code section 3601 addresses that situation. Subdivision (b) provides that the employer shall in no event be held liable, directly or indirectly, for damages awarded against or liability incurred by the other employee under those two exceptions. Cole v. Fair Oaks Fire Protection Dist. applied the pre-1982 version of this section to bar claims against the assistant chief as well as the district. California’s workers’ compensation system rests on a trade the California Supreme Court calls the “compensation bargain.” Labor Code section 3600, subdivision (a) imposes liability for workers’ compensation on an employer, without regard to negligence, for injuries arising out of and in the course of employment where the listed conditions of compensation concur, and it does so “in lieu of any other liability whatsoever” except as specifically provided in sections 3602, 3706 and 4558. Labor Code section 3602, subdivision (a) states the consequence: where section 3600’s conditions concur, the right to recover compensation is the sole and exclusive remedy of the employee against the employer. In Shoemaker v. Myers the Court described the theory behind those provisions — the employer takes on liability for industrial injury without regard to fault in exchange for a cap on the amount, and the employee gets relatively swift and certain benefits without having to prove fault but gives up the wider range of damages potentially available in tort. Section 3602, subdivision (c) marks the outer edge of the rule: in all cases where section 3600’s conditions of compensation do not concur, the employer’s liability is the same as if the workers’ compensation division had not been enacted. Whether the conditions of compensation concur as to any injury claimed by Jordan Lee is not addressed here.

expectedJSON.body: Cole v. Fair Oaks Fire Protection Dist. is the decision that set the test. A fire captain alleged that his assistant chief harassed him over union activity, falsely accused him of dishonesty, put him through what the complaint called a “kangaroo” disciplinary proceeding, publicly demoted him and stripped him of his badge, assigned him menial duties, and applied to force him into involuntary retirement; the stress raised his blood pressure and he suffered a disabling stroke. The California Supreme Court held the claim belonged in the workers’ compensation system. Its reasoning was that where the misconduct attributed to the employer consists of actions that are a normal part of the employment relationship — the Court named demotions, promotions, criticism of work practices, and frictions in negotiations as to grievances — an employee whose emotional distress causes disability cannot escape the exclusive remedy provisions by relabeling the employer’s decisions as manifestly unfair, outrageous, harassment, or intended to cause emotional disturbance. The Court explained why: if calling ordinary workplace conduct unfair or outrageous were enough, an employee could plead around exclusivity in every case merely by alleging an ulterior purpose of causing injury, which would be contrary to the compensation bargain. Applying that test to the facts before it, the Court described disciplinary hearings, demotions, friction over grievances, decisions to seek disability retirement, and demands to attend meetings that interfere with personal arrangements as an inherent part of the employment setting. How this test applies to anything that occurred between Jordan Lee and Acme, Inc. is not evaluated here.

Shoemaker also observed that the reach of the phrase “arising out of and in the course of the employment” is not cut off by the discharge itself, pointing to cases treating injuries suffered after a discharge — while retrieving tools or personal effects, or while discussing the reasons for the firing — as compensable. The California Supreme Court held that claims for intentional or negligent infliction of emotional distress are preempted by the exclusivity provisions of the workers’ compensation law notwithstanding the absence of any compensable physical disability. The Court called the physical-versus-emotional dichotomy logically insupportable and pointed out the perverse incentive it created, since the more severe the employer’s conduct and the more disabling the resulting distress, the more likely the employer would be shielded. It framed the governing rule instead in terms of two exceptions: so long as the basic conditions of compensation are otherwise satisfied and the employer’s conduct neither contravenes fundamental public policy nor exceeds the risks inherent in the employment relationship, an employee’s emotional distress injuries are subsumed under the exclusive remedy provisions. The Court also noted that the injury must still result in an industrial disability compensable under the workers’ compensation law. Whether any of this describes a claim of Jordan Lee is not addressed here.

expectedJSON.body: The exclusive remedy provisions do not reach every injury that happens at work. Shoemaker v. Myers collected the ways California courts have described the boundary, identifying the exclusive remedy provisions as inapplicable to conduct where the employer or insurer stepped out of their proper roles, or to conduct of an employer having a questionable relationship to the employment, and defining the category as conduct not stemming from a risk reasonably encompassed within the compensation bargain. Shoemaker itself applied that boundary to hold that an injury from a termination in retaliation for protected whistleblowing under the statute then before the Court lay well outside the compensation bargain. Light v. Department of Parks & Recreation collects that line and follows it. The Court of Appeal concluded that the workers’ compensation system was not the exclusive remedy for the plaintiff’s alleged injuries because they were based on conduct prohibited by the Fair Employment and Housing Act. Light concluded that, absent further guidance from the California Supreme Court, it was unwilling to abandon the longstanding view that unlawful discrimination and retaliation in violation of that Act falls outside the compensation bargain. expectedJSON.body: City of Moorpark v. Superior Court supplies a textual reason why statutory discrimination remedies are not swept into the workers’ compensation bar. A city employee was terminated after knee surgery and sued for disability discrimination under the Fair Employment and Housing Act and for common law wrongful discharge; the city argued that because her disability was work related, Labor Code section 132a was her exclusive remedy. The California Supreme Court disagreed, holding that section 132a does not provide the exclusive remedy for that type of discrimination and that Fair Employment and Housing Act and common law remedies are available. Part of its reasoning was structural. Labor Code section 3600 speaks of liability for “the compensation provided by this division,” and section 3207 defines compensation as compensation under division 4 of the Labor Code; section 132a sits in division 1. The Court concluded that the plain language of the exclusive remedy provisions apparently limits those provisions to division 4 remedies, and that remedies the Legislature placed in other divisions of the Labor Code are simply not subject to the workers’ compensation exclusive remedy provisions. The Court also reaffirmed that certain employer conduct falls outside the compensation bargain, citing Shoemaker’s holding that an injury from a whistleblower-retaliation termination lies well outside it and Gantt v. Sentry Insurance’s holding on common law wrongful discharge. Whether Jordan Lee has any claim under any of these provisions is not stated here.

expectedJSON.body: Saying that the workers’ compensation system is the exclusive remedy for a distress injury is not the same as saying the system will pay for it. Labor Code section 3208.3 sets separate thresholds for psychiatric injury. Subdivision (a) makes a psychiatric injury compensable if it is a mental disorder that causes disability or need for medical treatment and it is diagnosed under the prescribed criteria. Subdivision (b)(1) requires the employee to demonstrate by a preponderance of the evidence that actual events of employment were predominant as to all causes combined of the psychiatric injury, and subdivision (b)(2) lowers that showing to “a substantial cause” — defined in subdivision (b)(3) as at least 35 to 40 percent of the causation from all sources combined — for employees whose injuries resulted from being a victim of a violent act or from direct exposure to a significant violent act. Subdivision (c) states the Legislature’s intent to establish a new and higher threshold of compensability for psychiatric injury. Subdivision (d) bars compensation for a psychiatric injury unless the employee has been employed by that employer for at least six months, which need not be continuous, and does not apply where the injury is caused by a sudden and extraordinary employment condition; the same subdivision adds that nothing in it authorizes a damages action that would not otherwise exist under the exclusive remedy doctrine. Whether any injury claimed by Jordan Lee meets any of these thresholds is not evaluated here.

It states that no compensation under the workers’ compensation division shall be paid by an employer for a psychiatric injury if the injury was substantially caused by a lawful, nondiscriminatory, good faith personnel action, and that the burden of proof rests with the party asserting the issue. The three adjectives are cumulative on their face: the personnel action must be lawful, it must be nondiscriminatory, and it must be taken in good faith. The statute does not define “personnel action” or “good faith,” and it places the burden on whichever party raises the issue rather than automatically on the employer or the employee. Read alongside the exclusivity decisions described elsewhere in this sheet, subdivision (h) marks out a category of injury for which the workers’ compensation system is the exclusive remedy under those decisions and yet pays nothing under this subdivision. Labor Code section 3600, subdivision (a)(10) provides that, except for psychiatric injuries governed by section 3208.3, subdivision (e), where the claim for compensation is filed after notice of termination or layoff — including voluntary layoff — and the claim is for an injury occurring before the time of that notice, no compensation is to be paid unless the employee demonstrates by a preponderance of the evidence that one or more listed conditions apply. Those conditions include that the employer had notice of the injury before the notice of termination or layoff, that the employee’s pre-existing medical records contain evidence of the injury, or that the date of injury under Labor Code section 5411 or 5412 falls after the notice. Section 3208.3, subdivision (e) states a parallel rule for psychiatric injury, adding to the predominant-cause showing a requirement that one of five conditions exist, among them sudden and extraordinary events of employment, prior notice to the employer, pre-existing medical records evidencing treatment, or a finding of sexual or racial harassment by any trier of fact. Two limits appear in subdivision (g): a notice of termination or layoff that is not followed within 60 days by the termination or layoff is not subject to the rule, and the issuance of frequent notices of termination or layoff is to be considered a bad faith personnel action that makes the rule inapplicable to that employee. Whether notice given to Jordan Lee on June 12, 2026 triggers any of these provisions is not evaluated here.

expectedJSON.body: Employees who believe a particular manager caused the distress sometimes name that manager personally. Labor Code section 3601 addresses that situation. Subdivision (a) provides that where the conditions of compensation set forth in section 3600 concur, the right to recover workers’ compensation is, except as specifically provided in that section, the exclusive remedy for injury or death of an employee against any other employee of the employer acting within the scope of his or her employment. The section names two exceptions in which an action at law for damages against the other employee may be brought in addition to the compensation right against the employer: where the injury or death is proximately caused by the willful and unprovoked physical act of aggression of the other employee, and where it is proximately caused by the intoxication of the other employee. Subdivision (b) provides that the employer shall in no event be held liable, directly or indirectly, for damages awarded against or liability incurred by the other employee under those two exceptions. Cole v. Fair Oaks Fire Protection Dist. applied the pre-1982 version of this section to bar claims against the assistant chief as well as the district. Whether any individual is a proper defendant as to anything involving Jordan Lee is not addressed here.
